source.title: $M^3$ Scaling Law: Optimizing Multi-Epoch, Multi-Lingual, and Multi-Stage Training for Low-Resource Language Models
source.authors: Kosuke Akimoto; Taiki Miyagawa; M. Oyamada

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some tables and figures are flattened in the supplied text, but the reported results used below are assignable.
record.tranche_reason: It measures held-out target-language validation loss and evaluates scaling-law predictions on held-out splits, using a low-resource multilingual and multistage setup rather than the original scaling-law experiment.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own validation-loss fits, extrapolation scores, optimal-training analyses, and preliminary downstream-task correlations. Results cited from other work are not recorded. Detailed per-language/per-split R² values in Tables 9–12 and plotted values without separately stated numbers are not reproduced here; aggregate results and explicit textual findings are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own LLaMA models from scratch (about 1.5e7 to 9.4e8 non-embedding FLOPs/token, C0/16 to 2C0) in a low-resource multilingual, multi-epoch, multi-stage setting. It fits Chinchilla-based laws to held-out target-language validation loss and scores extrapolation to held-out larger-compute, larger-model and larger-data splits. It also derives compute-optimal model size and epoch count, and correlates validation loss with Japanese downstream scores. This is a new setting with its own results on V2, V3, V5, V6 and V7, so T3 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. M³ extrapolates to unseen hyperparameter regions better than the existing laws tested, across three language pairs. As DT shrinks, the optimal recipe switches directly from monolingual single-stage to multilingual two-stage, and multilingual single-stage is never optimal in their grid. Optimal epochs collapse onto one curve in DT/D*(C), exactly for a fixed ratio schedule and empirically when ratios are jointly optimized.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains LLaMA-architecture models from scratch on English/target-language C4 and mC4 data, varying epochs, language ratios, stages, model scale, and compute. This differs from the original general-purpose scaling-law setups and focuses on low-resource target-language validation loss.
record.method_sensitivity: Extrapolation changes with the scaling-law form and where (k,r) dependence is assigned: h versus hLp changes average R²; assigning dependence to RM* versus g trades off k-axis and M-axis accuracy. First-stage ratio dependence in γ2 gave no notable improvement. Compute-dependent learning-rate and batch-size schedules were fixed rather than searched.

fits_no_version.finding: In multi-stage training, loss depends only on the average and final-stage target-language ratios. The first-stage ratio and the internal split have negligible effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-stage pretraining loss is governed by average and final-stage data-mixture ratios, independent of intermediate schedule.

record.problems: One training run per setup due to compute constraints. Experiments use relatively small-scale models, three target-language/English pairs, fixed C4 and mC4 corpora, and do not search learning rate or batch size. Swahili has a restricted target-corpus range. Some extrapolation results are aggregate R² values; detailed per-language/per-split results are in tables not transcribed here. Downstream analysis is preliminary and uses small models.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-language/per-split R² values for every model and split in Tables 9–12 are not individually transcribed; aggregate results and principal ablations are included. Figure-only numerical points for loss landscapes, optimal ratios, and optimal model scale are omitted where the text gives no exact values. Table 2's additional per-axis values for comparator models and all setting-specific comparator averages beyond the selected key comparisons are omitted.

untested.parts: No fit quality is reported for the pure Chinchilla power law on non-bottlenecked runs. The study only uses fitted exponents inside its extended law, and model scale spans under two orders of magnitude.
Extrapolation to runs orders of magnitude larger is not tested. Held-out regions are only about 2 to 8 times beyond the training runs in C, M or D.
Kaplan and Hoffmann allocation exponents are not compared, and the parameter/token split is not estimated independently of the study's own fit.
Not tested at all. Shapes were fixed to aspect ratios of 30 to 150, following Kaplan.
Image, video and other modalities, and fine-tuning, are not tested.
Downstream scaling with model size or compute is not tested, nor any setting beyond small models.

missing.what: The effective-model-size saturation constant RM* falls with epoch count k, from about 100+ at k=2 to a floor, so the Muennighoff constant-saturation form is inadequate.
Fitting the Chinchilla base jointly with the other parameters makes the base parameters drift and substantially degrades M- and D-axis extrapolation. Two-phase fitting was adopted instead.
The full-data γ per language (0.0834, 0.0571, 0.0815) differs from the pilot single-stage γ of 0.1021, and γ2 also varies (0.0343, 0.0184, 0.0544).
NLI, entity linking and commonsense tasks had exact-match scores of almost consistently 0% at this scale.
Per-language, per-split R² includes strongly negative values for some laws and splits, especially Swahili.

record.verdict_notes: I changed the tranche from T2 to T3 because the method is standard law-fitting applied in a new setting. V1 gets no label: the rows give only fitted exponents, not fit quality of a plain power law, and repetition is a data bottleneck that V1 excludes. V5 was wrongly marked not_tested, since repeated data and multilingual/multi-stage regimes are tested directly. Comparator and ablation rows were moved from V2 to V7. Comparator laws lacking r, k or stage terms fail for missing variables, not because power-law extrapolation fails. r28 is a proof, not data. My own calculation from Table 13 (not reported by the authors): the implied data-allocation exponent α/(α+β) is about 0.54 for ja, 0.51 for id and 0.61 for sw, relevant to V3 and V7. Table 14's caption (+.05) disagrees with its values (.69 vs .67). The paper is single-run per setup and is a preprint.

versions.untested_parts: Tests loss modeling across model scale, data, compute, and recipe variables in low-resource target-language pretraining; does not establish the claim over several orders of magnitude in the standard unrestricted high-resource setting.
Tests held-out extrapolation across experimental hyperparameter splits in the tested low-resource setting, not extrapolation to runs orders of magnitude larger than all training runs.

Studies optimal epoch counts and training recipes under fixed compute and target-corpus budgets. It does not establish the standard unconstrained parameter-count/token-count compute-optimal split or compare Kaplan and Hoffmann allocation exponents.
Architecture depth, width, or shape effects at a fixed parameter count are not tested.
Other modalities and other training regimes such as repeated data beyond the tested text setup, fine-tuning, and transfer are not established.
Reports preliminary Japanese downstream-task correlations with validation loss; does not test downstream performance scaling with model size or compute, or establish predictability at larger scales.

Tests sensitivity to alternative effective-size and language-ratio formulations and reports extrapolation differences. It does not directly establish general disagreement between the original Kaplan and Hoffmann laws across their standard setups.

relationships.condition: Held-out larger compute and larger target corpus, plus monolingual multi-epoch held-out splits, within roughly 2 to 8 times of the training runs
relationships.reason: The M³ law reaches R² 0.79 on the C axis and 0.85 on the DT axis. The monolingual variant with k-dependent saturation reaches Avg 0.85, and the combined-stage d3 Avg is 0.74 (r09, r11, r23, r24).
